title: AtlasForge — Systems Onboard: SDK + Gateway + Burst Capacity Discovery
summary: Initial technical discovery to evaluate Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for AtlasForge's document ingestion assistant. Main concerns: rate limits during nightly batch ingests, gateway/proxy architecture to enforce quotas, LangChain/LlamaIndex integration patterns, observability hooks (tracing + token-level cost), and secure VPC/KMS options for private deployment.
topics: Deployment modes: hosted vs dedicated vs private
SDK integration patterns (node/python) and LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors
Gateway/proxy and sidecar options for request shaping
Rate limiting / quotas / burst capacity behavior
Observability hooks: traces, token breakdowns, alerts, webhooks
Security: KMS, VPC, SSO/SAML, audit logs

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-09-21
Time: 11:00 PT / 19:00 BST
Duration: 46m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions), Lina Morales (AtlasForge CTO), Ravi Singh (Platform), Tom Wu (DevOps), Priya Nair (Security)

Auto-summary (auto gen): AtlasForge is evaluating Redwood for an internal doc assistant. Key constraints: high nightly ingest bursts, need for strict quotas per internal team, want SDK-first integration and examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex, observability per-token cost, and private deployment options for data residency.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Ethan, our solutions engineer, and Jordan who helps with platform onboarding. Lina, thanks for the background doc you sent over, that was really helpful.
[00:18] Lina: Thanks, happy to be here. Quick note, we're dealing with a mix of real-time chat traffic and big nightly batch runs that push thousands of docs through embeddings. The batch spikes are our primary worry.
[00:33] Ethan: Got it. When you say "thousands," can you ballpark tokens per second or per run? Even an order of magnitude helps.
[00:40] Ravi: Right now nightly jobs hit about 2.5M tokens over a 10 minute window, so peak qps is kind of high for a short burst. Also we have concurrent interactive chats during the day with a much lower sustained qps.
[01:00] Maya: Perfect. That feeds right into the hosted vs dedicated conversation — hosted will throttle per-customer quotas and you can request burst increases but dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput.
[01:14] Tom: For us, predictability is important because our SLAs for internal ops teams are strict. But we also want to avoid paying for reserved capacity if we can use clever burst handling. How does Redwood handle burst capacity on hosted?
[01:30] Ethan: On hosted we have burst allowances; basically we smooth at the control plane level and you can request temporary burst increases. There's also smart routing where heavy requests can go to compatible quantized model variants to cut cost, but that can slightly increase latency.
[01:44] Priya: Can you explain the compatible model variants? We have compliance teams that care if the model behavior changes mid-run.
[01:52] Ethan: Sure. If the primary model isn't available or you're hitting a quota, Redwood can route to a variant — sometimes a quantized model or a smaller size — the idea is graceful degradation. We surface quality/regression metrics and you can pin model versions to avoid surprises. There's an audit log for routing decisions.
[02:12] Lina: Audit logs are non-negotiable. We need per-request traces and a token-level cost breakdown for chargebacks.
[02:20] Maya: We provide per-token cost breakdowns in the console and via webhooks. Also you can stream token-level events back into your observability pipeline. Ethan, maybe talk about tracing hooks?
[02:31] Ethan: Yeah, we have tracing integration: open telemetry spans around request lifecycle, token generation spans, and export to any OTLP collector. There's also a post-processing hook for token metadata if you want to attach user IDs.
[02:44] Ravi: Sweet. On integration, we're heavy into Python and LangChain. We also use LlamaIndex for retrieval. Do you have official SDKs and adapters?
[02:55] Ethan: Yes, official SDKs for Node and Python, and we maintain adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex. Quick note, some names in our docs can be stale, sometimes the community forks show up as "LangChannel" in older examples, so we'll give you the up-to-date snippets.
[03:12] Lina: Nice. For the embeddings pipeline — we want to run embeddings in the night job and then use those vectors in LlamaIndex during the day. Any suggestions on caching or rate shaping?
[03:24] Ethan: For embeddings we recommend batching large inputs and using asynchronous batching in the SDK. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching that aggregates short jobs to improve throughput. Also, consider prefix/KV caching — if you have repeated document prefixes, KV cache reduces token generation cost. But for embeddings, vectorization is mostly deterministic so you can cache vectors at application level.
[03:46] Tom: When you said KV cache earlier, you said KV "cash" in the doc I saw — that's OK, we laughed about it.
[03:52] (laughs)
[03:54] Maya: We've seen that transcription error elsewhere, it's classic.
[03:58] Priya: Security question: can Redwood run in our VPC or on-prem? We need to ensure KMS integration and that keys never leave our control.
[04:07] Ethan: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages. We integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support envelopes so you can hold root keys. For hosted we offer bring-your-own-key options via KMS integrations too, but it's different than fully private where the control plane is customer-managed.
[04:27] Lina: If we go private, what's the effort to spin up? Does it require a long lead time like months?
[04:33] Jordan: Typical private deployments for customers with our standard stack can be weeks for the majority of the infra, but fully air-gapped or on-prem with HSM provisioning can extend that. We do a checklist: networking, KMS, audit endpoints, and can provide deployment runbooks.
[04:50] Ravi: OK. Another pattern we want is a gateway in front of Redwood so our teams can enforce per-team quotas and route requests through a proxy with auth. Do you see customers using a sidecar vs an API gateway approach?
[05:04] Ethan: Both. The gateway approach (API gateway) centralizes routing and rate limiting. Sidecar approach brings per-service controls. Redwood also offers a lightweight proxy pattern we call the "redwood gateway adapter" — it's essentially a small proxy that enforces quotas then forwards to the Redwood API, and it can be deployed in your k8s cluster. That adapter supports token-level tagging for observability.
[05:26] Tom: Does that adapter add noticeable latency for short chat requests? Our interactivity target is 200ms p95 so extra hops are concerning.
[05:34] Ethan: The adapter is designed to be low-latency — typically adds 8-20ms depending on your network. The bigger factors are batching and the model's generation time. For 200ms p95 you may want dedicated capacity and a small model with optimization flags; we can tune kernel selection and sequence length.
[05:55] Lina: Where does rate limiting occur? Client-side? Gateway? Redwood control plane?
[06:01] Maya: You can choose. If you use the gateway, you enforce at your edge. Redwood enforces per-account quotas in the control plane — and dedicated customers can have soft/hard limits with burst windows configured. We also have tokens per-route limits if you want fine-grained control.
[06:17] Ravi: We're interested in per-team quotas and per-route budgets. For example, Analytics team gets X tokens per month, Ops gets Y. Can Redwood do token-level chargebacks?
[06:27] Ethan: Yes, we provide token-level usage logs with route tags so you can attribute cost. Many customers import that into their internal billing. We also have SDK hooks to set route metadata per request which appears in traces and cost reports.
[06:44] Lina: On the SDKs — can we inject route metadata and do automatic retries with backoff? Our current client library expects idempotency.
[06:51] Ethan: SDKs support custom headers for metadata, request id, and have configurable retry/backoff strategies out of the box. Idempotency tokens are supported for generation and embeddings endpoints.
[07:03] Tom: For the nightly large ingest — would you recommend spinning up a dedicated pool for that window or use hosted burst and accept slower completion?
[07:10] Ethan: It depends on how important predictability and latency are. If the window is critical and you can't tolerate queuing, reserved capacity is the clean option. If you can tolerate some spillover and cost sensitivity matters, hosted with scheduled burst windows and adaptive routing will work. We can run a short benchmark to see cost delta.
[07:29] Lina: We definitely want to see numbers. Can Redwood run a benchmark against our sample workload?
[07:33] Maya: Yes, we ask for a traffic profile sample and we'll run an eval on hosted and dedicated. Ethan will help scope the benchmark plan.
[07:40] Ethan: For benchmarking we'll need: a) representative request shapes (payload sizes), b) sequence length distribution, c) target p95 latency, d) desired throughput for the batch. With that we can simulate and give cost/latency tradeoffs.
[07:56] Ravi: We'll share that. A few more integration questions: How do you handle streaming and function calling? We rely on streaming for our UI and function calls to hit internal services.
[08:06] Ethan: Streaming is supported in the SDK and the API — you can open a streaming connection and get partial tokens. For function-call style structured outputs we support JSON schema enforcement and structured output options. We also support hooks to call out to external tools during generation via function calling.
[08:21] Priya: For audit we need to retain logs for 7 years, including who initiated the request. Do you store user info in Redwood logs?
[08:30] Maya: We store request metadata and you can push logs to your storage using webhooks or S3 export. For private deployments you can keep everything in your own audit store. On hosted we have retention tiers and enterprise plans that extend retention and give search access.
[08:44] Lina: Any gotchas with LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters? We've hit weird behaviors with callback managers and retrievers in the past.
[08:53] Ethan: Common issues are mismatch of tokenization and chunk sizes for retrievers, and callback managers that duplicate events. We provide a sample repo that shows recommended chunk sizes, retriever tuning, and how to wire the SDK's streaming callbacks into LangChain's callback manager. We'll send that sample.
[09:08] Jordan: Also watch out for model leading tokens if you add system prompts across many calls, that can bloat token counts — the repo has utilities to compute rolling token counts.
[09:18] Ravi: Good to know. On observability we want direct export to our Datadog and a Slack alert if cost spikes exceed a threshold. Can Redwood push to Datadog and trigger alerts?
[09:28] Ethan: Yes, we have built-in integrations: Datadog, Prometheus metrics, OTLP, and webhooks. You can configure alerts based on token rates or error rates, and webhooks can trigger Slack. For hosted customers we also expose dashboards in the Redwood Console.
[09:42] Tom: Is there an API to pull historical token usage for the last 12 months?
[09:47] Maya: Yes, usage APIs and exports. For long-term retention you can set up daily exports to S3 and query from there.
[09:56] Lina: Let's cover network egress. If we go private in our VPC, is traffic internal or does it still egress?
[10:04] Jordan: In private deployments traffic stays in your network; we don't egress. In hosted with VPC peering you can keep traffic in-region but there will be cloud-provider egress considerations depending on topology.
[10:17] Priya: Compliance — do you have SOC2 and ISO? Also, can we get a penetration test report?
[10:24] Maya: Redwood holds SOC 2 Type II, and we have ISO in progress. We can share redacted pen test reports under an NDA and provide our security whitepaper.
[10:35] Lina: Great. Back to quotas: does Redwood support soft limits with email notification and hard limits that block? We want both behaviors per route.
[10:44] Ethan: Yes — soft/hard limit pairs are configurable. Soft triggers can create alerts or slow down, hard limits return 429. You can also set per-route and per-user quotas.
[10:55] Ravi: For 429s, do you provide a recommended backoff header or Retry-After?
[10:59] Ethan: Yes, standard Retry-After headers and we include a payload indicating quota metadata. SDKs automatically respect Retry-After if configured.
[11:09] Tom: Any customers running the gateway adapter in k8s with Istio or envoy? We use envoy and want compatibility.
[11:15] Ethan: Yes, many customers run the adapter as a sidecar with envoy filters; it's compatible. We have an example Helm chart and envoy filter snippets in the repo.
[11:25] Lina: About price — high-level question: for embeddings and generation cost structure? Are embeddings billed per vector or per token?
[11:33] Maya: Embeddings are billed per embedding unit (typically per example) and generation is per token. We'll send a clear price table.
[11:40] Priya: One last security nuance — do you do encrypted logs at rest in hosted?
[11:45] Maya: Yes, hosted logs are encrypted at rest. For additional controls we suggest private with your KMS.
[11:52] (10m mark)
[11:54] Ethan: Quick technical note: for your nightly ingest if you plan to run 2.5M tokens in 10 minutes, we should simulate the concurrency—whether it's thousands of concurrent requests or fewer large batched requests. Different behaviors change the recommended kernel selection and batching config.
[12:08] Ravi: It's many concurrent small requests from our workers. We'll attach a trace sample.
[12:13] Ethan: Great. We'll include a recommended batching config that reduces per-token cost and keeps latency bounds.
[12:20] Lina: For the pilot, what's a reasonable success criteria? We were thinking: a) under 300ms p95 for chat, b) nightly ingest completes within 15 minutes, c) token cost reduces or at least predictable, and d) logs and traces are available in our Datadog.
[12:35] Maya: That's a good list. We'll scope the pilot to validate those metrics.
[12:40] Tom: Who should we loop in next? On our side we'll bring infra and security. Lina will own the internal coordination.
[12:46] Lina: Yep, I'll schedule the deep dive.
[12:50] Maya: Recap and next steps — we'll send pricing, LangChain/LlamaIndex samples, adapter repo, and a benchmark plan. Athena — sorry Ethan — will set up the benchmark plan with your sample workload. We'll come back with a pilot proposal.
[13:06] Ravi: Thanks. One tiny question: do you support on-the-fly quantization or do you provide pre-quantized model variants?
[13:12] Ethan: We provide pre-quantized variants that are tested; on-the-fly quantization is experimental and not recommended for production.
[13:20] Priya: Ok that helps. Anything else?
[13:23] (brief pause)
[13:24] Maya: Nothing from Redwood. Lina, thanks for time; we'll follow up with the materials by Friday.
[13:30] Lina: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

--- End transcript ---
